package_info.package_manager: N/A (malware binary, not a package manager ecosystem)
package_info.why_malicious: The CrySIS/Dharma ransomware family is designed to encrypt user files, delete system recovery data, persist across reboots, and extort victims for payment. Its behavior is intentionally destructive and criminal, with no legitimate use case.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: SetConsoleCP(1251); // Set codepage to support Cyrillic languages
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code sets the console codepage to 1251, enabling Cyrillic character support for displaying ransom notes to Russian-speaking victims, resulting in readable extortion instructions.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Changing the console codepage to a Cyrillic locale is uncommon for most software and is typically only done for localization. In ransomware, this is used to ensure ransom notes are displayed in the attacker's preferred language.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software does not alter the system codepage unless specifically required for legitimate localization; ransomware does this to ensure ransom instructions are readable to targeted victims.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Internationalized software may set codepages for proper language display, but only when the user selects a non-default language.
key_indicators: Explicit call to SetConsoleCP(1251)
Preparation for non-English ransom note display
Localization to Russian/Cyrillic users

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes vssadmin.exe with arguments to silently delete all shadow copies, removing system restore points and preventing file recovery by the victim.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Deleting all shadow copies is a well-known anti-recovery tactic used by ransomware to prevent victims from restoring files without paying the ransom.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software should not delete all system backups or shadow copies without explicit user consent and clear notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup management tools may delete old or corrupted shadow copies as part of scheduled maintenance, but not all at once and not silently.
key_indicators: Execution of vssadmin.exe with Delete Shadows /All /Quiet
Silent removal of all shadow copies
Disabling system recovery options

required_permissions: write access to user startup folders

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code copies its own binary to the user's Startup folder, ensuring the ransomware will execute automatically on system reboot, thereby maintaining persistence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Self-replication to the Startup folder is a classic persistence mechanism for malware, allowing it to survive reboots and continue malicious activity.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate installers may add shortcuts for auto-start, but do not copy the main executable itself for persistence without user approval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications add auto-start entries via shortcuts or registry keys, but rarely by copying the main binary directly.
key_indicators: Self-copy of executable to Startup folder
Persistence mechanism via Startup folder
Unauthorized modification of user Startup directory

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: For each file in user directories: Encrypt file and append custom extension
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code iterates through user directories, encrypts each file using a cryptographic algorithm, and appends a custom extension to the filename, rendering files inaccessible to the victim.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mass file encryption with custom extensions is the core behavior of ransomware, directly resulting in data loss and extortion.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not encrypt user files in bulk without explicit user intent and clear notification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Encryption utilities may encrypt files, but only with user initiation and consent, and typically do not append random or variant-specific extensions.
key_indicators: Bulk file encryption across user directories
Custom extension appended to encrypted files
Automated, non-user-initiated encryption process

required_permissions: write access to multiple system/user directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Write Info.hta to: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, C:\Users\<victim>\AppData\Roaming, C:\Users\<victim>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup, C:\Windows\System32
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code writes a ransom note (Info.hta) to multiple system and user directories, ensuring the victim is presented with payment instructions upon login or system start.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping ransom notes in multiple prominent locations is a hallmark of ransomware, maximizing the likelihood that the victim will see the attacker's demands.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not create ransom notes or demand payment, nor does it write .hta files to system directories without user consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may place informational files in user directories, but not with extortion content or in .hta format.
key_indicators: Creation of Info.hta in multiple system/user directories
Use of .hta file for ransom instructions
Files written to Startup and System32 folders

required_permissions: write access to root and desktop directories

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Write info.txt to: C:\, C:\Users\Public\Desktop, C:\Users\<victim>\Desktop
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code writes a text file (info.txt) containing attacker contact instructions to the root directory and desktop locations, making ransom payment details highly visible to the victim.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Dropping contact instructions in prominent locations is a common ransomware tactic to ensure the victim is aware of the extortion demand.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not demand ransom or provide criminal contact information in user-accessible directories.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may place readme or info files on the desktop, but not with extortion or criminal content.
key_indicators: info.txt with attacker contact details
Files placed in root and desktop directories
Presence of ransom instructions in plain text

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After encryption, the code launches mshta.exe with Info.hta as an argument, immediately displaying the ransom note to the victim via a Windows HTML Application.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching mshta.exe to display a ransom note is a direct and automated method to ensure the victim sees payment instructions, leveraging a built-in Windows utility.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not use mshta.exe to display extortion messages or launch ransom notes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some enterprise tools may use mshta.exe for legitimate HTML-based utilities, but not for extortion or ransom note display.
key_indicators: mshta.exe execution with Info.hta
Immediate display of ransom note upon encryption completion
Automated launch of HTML Application for extortion

attack_chain.action: Initial execution of ransomware binary, sets codepage for ransom note display.
Deletes shadow copies to prevent file recovery.
Copies itself to Startup folder for persistence.
Encrypts user files and appends custom extension.
Drops ransom notes (Info.hta, info.txt) in multiple locations.
Launches mshta.exe to display ransom note to victim.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of vssadmin.exe with Delete Shadows /All /Quiet to remove all shadow copies
Self-copying of ransomware binary to Startup folders for persistence
Bulk file encryption with custom, variant-specific extensions
Dropping and launching Info.hta via mshta.exe for ransom note display
Creation of ransom notes (Info.hta, info.txt) in multiple user and system directories
file_indicators: Presence of Info.hta in Startup, System32, and user AppData folders
info.txt in root (C:\), C:\Users\Public\Desktop, and C:\Users\<victim>\Desktop
Files with new, unusual extensions specific to ransomware variant
Ransomware binary present in Startup folder
network_indicators: CrySIS/Dharma typically does not exfiltrate data, but ransom notes may include attacker email addresses or chat service links for payment communication; monitor for outbound connections to these addresses as specified in ransom notes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of vssadmin.exe with arguments to delete shadow copies, creation of Info.hta and info.txt in system and user directories, mass file renaming with new extensions, and execution of mshta.exe with Info.hta as an argument. Alert on binaries self-replicating to Startup folders and on the sudden appearance of ransom notes or bulk file encryption activity. Correlate with the presence of attacker contact details in newly created files.
